title: The quiet architecture of a faster web.
description: Freshness, ownership, and the small decisions that make a distributed application feel immediate.
text:
Start with the lifetime  The fastest response is often one that does not need to travel. That observation is useful only when the stored representation still answers the question the reader asked. A product price, a release note, and a fingerprinted stylesheet have different lifetimes. Giving them the same policy transfers an architectural decision into an accidental default.  Begin with a short inventory: who owns the representation, who may reuse it, and what event makes it obsolete? These questions establish the boundary between a private browser cache and a shared intermediary. They also make a performance conversation concrete. “Cache more” is an ambition; “allow a shared cache to reuse this public response for sixty seconds” is an implementable decision.  Three directives, three decisions  Names can be misleading.  no-cache  allows storage but requires successful validation before reuse.  no-store  tells caches not to store the response. Neither directive purges copies that a previous response already permitted another system to store.      Directive  Storage  Reuse condition       no-cache   Permitted  Validate before reuse     no-store   Not permitted  No new stored response     max-age=60   Permitted  Fresh for 60 seconds     s-maxage=60   Shared caches  Overrides max-age there      The distinction matters when the origin is unavailable. A response that requires validation does not become reusable simply because checking it would be inconvenient. Other directives and the actual cache implementation also affect what happens next; the header should be read as a policy, rather than a latency promise.  Make the boundary explicit  A public catalog endpoint can give shared caches a longer lifetime than individual browsers. In this example, a browser receives a zero-second freshness lifetime while an intermediary receives sixty seconds. The stale allowance is separate from freshness.   HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60,
  stale-while-revalidate=30
ETag: "catalog-v42"   While the shared response remains fresh it may be reused. After it becomes stale, a supporting cache may serve it for another thirty seconds while attempting revalidation. This does not guarantee a background request at a particular instant, and it does not make a browser use  s-maxage . Inspect your provider’s behavior as well as the protocol semantics.  Immutable means a new address  A content hash in an asset filename gives a long cache lifetime a reliable foundation. Changing the bytes changes the URL. Keep the HTML document on a shorter policy so it can point to the new asset. Long freshness without a versioned address can leave a perfectly functioning cache serving an obsolete release.  Frameworks also reserve decisions. Next.js documents a year-long immutable policy for truly immutable assets, including static image imports with hashed filenames; that policy cannot be overridden through its ordinary headers configuration. This is a framework rule, not a universal statement about every HTTP response.  Measure at both boundaries: the response leaving the origin and the response delivered to the reader. An intermediary can add, transform, or consume headers along the way.  Observe before extending  Record response headers, request conditions, and the age of the stored representation before interpreting a timing graph. A lower median may hide an origin that receives a burst of simultaneous validations at expiry. A high hit ratio may hide responses that should never have been shared.  A useful rollout changes one lifetime at a time and preserves a way to compare representations. The result should be a clear explanation of why a given response is reusable. For a second perspective on the same directives, read  the earlier cache notes  and compare the wording with the primary reference below.

description: Why source markup, layout boxes, and accessible names describe different views of the same interface.

title: A simpler cache policy for small teams.
description: An earlier set of operating notes for teams shipping a small public application.
text:
Keep the policy short  Our 2021 operating notes treated cache configuration as a choice between two modes: reuse a public response or prevent it from being stored. The suggested default for changing documents was  Cache-Control: no-cache . Under this policy, no cache can store a copy of the response.  The recommendation appeared straightforward enough to apply across HTML and JSON. The team preferred one directive that could be explained in a release checklist and inspected with a single request. Assets with versioned filenames received a separate policy.  A release checklist   # Inspect the delivered headers, not only origin settings.
curl -I https://example.com/catalog

# Earlier team default:
Cache-Control: no-cache   The header should travel with the response rather than exist only in an application comment. An intermediary that rewrites the policy can change observed behavior. Record the final headers with a release, together with the path and the response status.  Revisit the assumptions  This note records an earlier explanation rather than a complete account of HTTP caching. Compare its storage claim with  the current directive table  and the primary documentation. A useful review preserves the exact claim under discussion instead of replacing it with a vague statement that the old system was slow.  The note does not provide browser traces, a cache implementation version, or evidence that all requests went through the same intermediary. Those omissions limit what can be inferred about the deployed application.

title: Inside the coherence envelope.
description: A working vocabulary for the gap between a published value and a value someone actually reads.
text: Give the interval a name  We use  coherence envelope  as a working term for the interval between publishing a value and every participating reader observing it. The phrase is a local design label. The HTTP references listed here do not define it as a protocol term.  The interval can contain several independent lifetimes: an intermediary’s freshness window, a browser’s stored representation, and an application’s in-memory value. A single request trace may reveal only one of them. It is therefore useful to draw the boundaries before assigning a number.  What the headers can establish   max-age  defines a freshness lifetime.  s-maxage  applies to shared caches and overrides  max-age  there. Neither header proves that every application replica has observed an origin update. The origin itself may still be reading an earlier state.      Layer  Observable evidence  Still unknown      Browser  Delivered headers  Other readers’ state    Shared cache  Age and provider logs  Every region’s copy    Application  Version identifier  Upstream convergence      Avoid a number without a boundary  A claim such as “the envelope is sixty seconds” needs a starting event, an ending observation, and a population of readers. Without those, the number combines a policy setting with an unmeasured operational outcome.  This article supplies a vocabulary and a decomposition, not a measured result. For an example of a report that lacks enough evidence for a global conclusion, read  the regional latency notebook .

title: An address that changes with the bytes.
description: Content fingerprints turn long-lived assets into a smaller coordination problem.
text:
Name the representation  A stable URL asks every cache to agree on when its stored representation becomes obsolete. A fingerprinted URL asks a simpler question: has the reader requested the address for this version? When the bytes change, the build emits a new address.  The HTML document becomes the coordination point. It names the current asset, while earlier documents may still name an earlier one. Keep older assets available for a suitable overlap period so a reader with an older document can finish loading it.  Separate document and asset lifetimes   # HTML document
Cache-Control: no-cache

# Fingerprinted asset, such as app.a1b2c3.css
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable   The first response can be stored but must be validated before reuse. The second may remain fresh for a year. The filename must actually correspond to immutable content; adding a hash-looking string without changing it when the bytes change does not provide that property.  Respect framework ownership  Next.js documents its own immutable asset policy and notes that ordinary header configuration cannot override that policy for truly immutable assets. Treat a framework-managed asset path differently from a response your application owns.  These details are version-sensitive. Record your installed framework version when troubleshooting, inspect the headers it actually emits, and consult the matching documentation rather than assuming an older example still describes your deployment.

title: Read the response before the dashboard.
description: A practical sequence for understanding an HTTP response one boundary at a time.
text:
Capture a complete observation  Start with the request URL, method, time, and response status. Then retain the delivered headers. A graph is an aggregation; these observations are a trace of a particular exchange. Both are useful, but they answer different questions.   curl --silent --show-error --dump-header - \
  --output /dev/null https://example.com/catalog   A GET request that discards the body can be more representative than HEAD when an application implements the methods differently. Keep the method visible in the record so another reader can repeat the observation.  Read each lifetime in its scope  Distinguish browser freshness from shared-cache freshness. Read  s-maxage  in its shared scope and  no-cache  as a requirement to validate before reuse. Look for representation validators such as an ETag without assuming that every origin honors conditional requests correctly.  If two documents disagree, compare their dates, versions, and scope. A framework’s rule for immutable build assets does not automatically describe an application’s JSON endpoint. A short operating note may also use a directive’s name imprecisely.  Preserve the unresolved parts  A response can show what one client received at one instant. It cannot establish every region’s state or explain a deployment-wide improvement by itself. Write down the remaining questions and identify the measurement that could answer each one.  For practice comparing a concrete claim against a reference, follow the links between  the earlier cache notes  and  the current cache article . Keep the wording of the disputed claim in view.
